Chapter 50

What I would do next, and what you now know

The project is complete and the suite is green, and it is still version one. An honest list of the next ten pieces of work, each with the chapter it would touch, then every deferred item with the reason it waits — generated, and checked against the exit criteria; a map from every Svelte and SvelteKit capability the course used to the chapter that used it; and how to keep the project current as the framework moves.

By the end of this chapter

Leave with a prioritised backlog you could start on tomorrow, a mental index of where each framework feature lives in the code, and a routine for upgrading without breaking the course.

A course that ends with “and now it is done” is lying to you. Software is finished when it is deleted; until then it has a backlog, and a good backlog is the most honest description of a project’s state. This one is ordered by what a real trip-planning team would ask for first, and every item names the chapter whose code it would change, because the chapters were written so that this list could be short.

The next ten

  1. Notice a sign-out in another tab. Sign out in one tab and the others still look signed in until they next ask the server for something — mutations already answer 401 and the toast says so, but the page should know first. The shape is depends('meridian:session') on the layout’s load and an invalidate when the tab becomes visible again (chapter 25). The live stream has the same gap at a smaller scale: it re-checks *membership* on every wake (chapter 19), but the person on locals is the one the connection opened with. (B4-D30)
  2. Prove the redirect sanitiser. redirectTo is cleaned rather than rejected (chapter 47), and nothing yet proves //evil.example lands on /trips. One end-to-end test, and LoadEvent.untrack so the guard does not re-run on every navigation. (B4-D55)
  3. A sitemap. A prerendered sitemap.xml/+server.ts with an hreflang alternate per language, for four guides in three languages (chapter 36). Fifteen minutes. (B4-D57)
  4. Rate-limit the public surface. Sign-in, sign-up, the join page and the route API are reachable by anyone. A token bucket on getClientAddress() in the security handler, answering 429 with retry-after, and ADDRESS_HEADER / XFF_DEPTH read correctly behind the proxy (chapters 47, 48). The end-to-end suite signs in from one address many times, so it needs a limit per environment. (B4-D62)
  5. A cover image for a trip. An upload is fields.cover.as('file') with v.file() and a size cap, sharp for the resizing, an endpoint to serve it, and BODY_SIZE_LIMIT raised to match (chapter 48). Not as('image'), which sounds right and is <input type="image"> — click coordinates, ImageInputValue, no file at all. (B4-D54)
  6. A share image. render() from svelte/server drawing the route as an SVG in an endpoint, and og:image on the trip page (chapter 38). (B4-D50)
  7. Stops mentioned in the notes. A Tiptap node view that renders a Svelte component with mount and unmount — the one honest place for them in this project (chapter 32). Two new dependencies and the biggest item here. (B4-D51)
  8. Installable. A web manifest and an icon set; the worker that installing needs is already there (chapter 39). (B3-D1)
  9. Writing offline. Note saves queued while the network is gone and replayed on online, with a conflict policy against the live query’s last-writer-wins (chapters 39, 19). (B3-D5)
  10. An inventory from the compiler. A scripts/inventory.ts that walks every component with parse from svelte/compiler and writes the map of features from what the code actually uses, so chapter 05 is generated rather than kept (chapter 45). (B1-D2)

Further out, the work a growing product would ask for rather than the work this course left: invites sent by email from an outbox written in the same transaction (chapter 20); a libSQL server instead of a file, and rooms on a pub/sub two processes share (chapters 14, 19); the traces exported to an OTLP collector (chapter 37); a fourth, right-to-left locale (chapter 21); a session with a real screen reader on the drag-and-drop; a tile server behind a flag. And one upgrade with a date on it: mdsvex 1.0, the first release to write <script module>, when it leaves prerelease (chapter 45).

Three things are deliberately *not* on the list. A native app: the map and the globe already work on a phone, and a web manifest is item eight. A rewrite of the itinerary as a CRDT: the live query with last-write-wins per stop is the right trade for a few people planning a trip. And a second framework for the marketing pages: the home page is a SvelteKit route like the others, prerendered where it can be.

The whole list

The ten above are the top of a longer list: every piece of work the course planned and decided not to do yet, each with the reason it waits. It is generated from the gap list that decided what this course would build, and checked on every build — the exit criteria in chapter 51 mark a surface *deferred* only if its item is here, and where the row says the item names the surface, the item’s own text has to. The ids are the gap list’s own: B1 is the toolchain, B2 design and motion, B3 offline, B4 the server and the pages, B5 the proofs; so “goes with B4-D8” points at a row of this table.

Where everything lives

This is the index of the course by *capability* rather than by feature — the list to keep open when you start your own project and want to remember where a thing was done properly.

  • Runes — $state, $derived, $derived.by, $effect, $props, $props.id(), $state.raw, $state.snapshot, assignable $derived: chapters 07, 26, 27, 33. untrack and the effect-loop it prevents: ch. 26; untrack inside an attachment, so a snapshot does not rebuild an editor: ch. 32. Classes with runes in .svelte.ts: ch. 07, 26. (No $bindable: no component here offers two-way binding as its API, so none declares it.)

  • Routing and loading — route groups: ch. 25; defineParams matchers: ch. 15, and the typed params a page takes through PageProps, with LayoutProps for a layout: ch. 25, 26; resolve() with typed route ids including groups, and paths.relative: false so the server writes paths too: ch. 25, 37; entries() with prerender and csr = false: ch. 36, 38; reroute for locales: ch. 21; +server.ts endpoints with CORS and OPTIONS: ch. 38, 47; the root layout with no load so prerendered pages do not bake a user in: ch. 25.

Keeping it current

The framework this course is built on moves every few weeks, and the versions in chapter 40 are dated for that reason. The routine above is the whole upgrade process. On a major version it starts with two more lines: read the migration guide — get-documentation with ["kit/migrating-to-sveltekit-3"], from an agent through the MCP server or from the terminal through the same package’s CLI — and then npx sv migrate, one task per commit, before pnpm update touches anything else (chapter 49). The reason the routine is short is the reason the tests exist: verify is the same command in the pipeline and on a laptop, the suite runs against the built output, and the course reads the code rather than copying it — so a refactor that moves a function changes the course the next time it is built, and verify.js says which ranges need a human. When a SvelteKit release renames a thing, the Svelte documentation server and the svelte-autofixer used throughout this series are the fastest way to learn the new name; when it adds a thing, the question to ask is the one from chapter 01: is this the right shape, does it earn its bytes, could we remove it later.

You have built a collaborative application with a real-time document, three languages, a map, a globe, a shared ledger, an editor, a public API, an embeddable element, a published library, a container and a pipeline — and you have read every line of it with the reason beside the code. That is what “state of the art” means in practice: not the newest thing, but the right thing, chosen on purpose, and proven.

Checkpoint

  • You can pick one item from the backlog and name the files it would change before opening the editor.
  • You can find the chapter for any capability in the map above without searching.
  • You can run the upgrade routine end to end, including the two lines a major version adds, and say what each command protects.
